claim: pickpocket 29 (ppk29) encodes a Drosophila degenerin/epithelial sodium channel (DEG/ENaC)
source: Here we show that pickpocket 29 (ppk29), a gene that encodes a Drosophila degenerin/epithelial sodium channel (DEG/ENaC), regulates neuronal excitability via a protein-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Liu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Zelle et al., 2013) in the Results section.

claim: ppk29 regulates neuronal excitability via a protein-independent mechanism
source: Here we show that pickpocket 29 (ppk29), a gene that encodes a Drosophila degenerin/epithelial sodium channel (DEG/ENaC), regulates neuronal excitability via a protein-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data showing that the 3'UTR alone can rescue phenotypes.

claim: The mRNA 3′UTR of ppk29 affects neuronal firing rates
source: We demonstrate that the mRNA 3′UTR of ppk29 affects neuronal firing rates and associated heat-induced seizures by acting as a natural antisense transcript (NAT) that regulates the neuronal mRNA levels of seizure (sei), the Drosophila homolog of the human Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (hERG) potassium channel.
evidence: Supported by neurophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B,C and transgenic rescue experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: The mRNA 3′UTR of ppk29 affects heat-induced seizures
source: We demonstrate that the mRNA 3′UTR of ppk29 affects neuronal firing rates and associated heat-induced seizures by acting as a natural antisense transcript (NAT) that regulates the neuronal mRNA levels of seizure (sei), the Drosophila homolog of the human Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (hERG) potassium channel.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3A and transgenic rescue experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: ppk29 mRNA acts as a natural antisense transcript (NAT) that regulates the neuronal mRNA levels of seizure (sei)
source: We demonstrate that the mRNA 3′UTR of ppk29 affects neuronal firing rates and associated heat-induced seizures by acting as a natural antisense transcript (NAT) that regulates the neuronal mRNA levels of seizure (sei), the Drosophila homolog of the human Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (hERG) potassium channel.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing sei mRNA levels change with ppk29 manipulation (Figure 3E,F, Figure 5C) and by the requirement for Dicer-2 (Figure 5E,F).

claim: seizure (sei) is the Drosophila homolog of the human Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (hERG) potassium channel
source: We demonstrate that the mRNA 3′UTR of ppk29 affects neuronal firing rates and associated heat-induced seizures by acting as a natural antisense transcript (NAT) that regulates the neuronal mRNA levels of seizure (sei), the Drosophila homolog of the human Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (hERG) potassium channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work (Titus et al., 1997; Wang et al., 1997).

claim: The regulatory impact of ppk29 mRNA on sei is independent of the sodium channel it encodes
source: We find that the regulatory impact of ppk29 mRNA on sei is independent of the sodium channel it encodes.
evidence: Supported by transgenic experiments showing that ppk29 3'UTR alone can rescue the ppk29 mutation phenotype (Figure 4C) and pharmacological blocking of SEI channels (Figure 4A).

claim: The neuronal action potential is sensitive to abrupt changes in environmental temperatures
source: The neuronal action potential is sensitive to abrupt changes in environmental temperatures (Peng et al., 2007; Buzatu, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The failure of neurons to adjust their physiological properties in response to a fast rise in temperature can lead to neurological disorders such as febrile seizures
source: Thus, the failure of neurons to adjust their physiological properties in response to a fast rise in temperature can lead to neurological disorders such as febrile seizures (Bassan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Maintaining normal neuronal excitability under varying environmental temperatures depends on changes in the abundance and membrane half-life of various voltage-dependent ion channels
source: Previous theoretical and experimental studies suggested that one of the main mechanisms for maintaining normal neuronal excitability, circuit integrity, and behavioral robustness under varying environmental temperatures depends on changes in the abundance and membrane half-life of various voltage-dependent ion channels (Marder and Prinz, 2003; O'Leary et al., 2013; Rinberg et al., 2013; Rosati and McKinnon, 2004; Tang et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: The actual molecular mechanisms that mediate changes in ion channel abundance and membrane half-life in response to temperature are largely unknown
source: However, the actual molecular mechanisms that mediate these processes are largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, inferred from the lack of prior mechanistic studies.

claim: Natural antisense non-coding transcripts (NATs) are prevalent in eukaryotes
source: Several whole genome transcriptomics studies revealed that natural antisense non-coding transcripts (NATs) are prevalent in eukaryotes (Lapidot and Pilpel, 2006; Okamura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to whole genome transcriptomics studies.

claim: At least some cis-NATs are likely to act as regulatory RNAs of protein-coding transcripts
source: Although the function of the majority of NATs is still unknown, evidence suggests that at least some cis-NATs are likely to act as regulatory RNAs of protein-coding transcripts (Borsani et al., 2005; Okamura et al., 2008; Watanabe et al., 2008), including a recent report about a non-coding NAT that regulates a neuronal potassium channel (Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies showing regulatory functions of NATs.

claim: A non-coding NAT regulates a neuronal potassium channel
source: Although the function of the majority of NATs is still unknown, evidence suggests that at least some cis-NATs are likely to act as regulatory RNAs of protein-coding transcripts (Borsani et al., 2005; Okamura et al., 2008; Watanabe et al., 2008), including a recent report about a non-coding NAT that regulates a neuronal potassium channel (Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent report.

claim: Some NATs have been shown to play a role in the physiological response to various stresses in plants
source: Furthermore, some NATs have been shown to play a role in the physiological response to various stresses in plants (Borsani et al., 2005; Katiyar-Agarwal et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies in plants.

claim: seizure (sei) encodes the sole fly homolog of the human Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (hERG) inward rectifying K+ channel
source: Using this approach, we found that the gene seizure (sei), which encodes the sole fly homolog of the human Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (hERG) inward rectifying K+ channel (Titus et al., 1997; Wang et al., 1997), is located downstream of the degenerin/epithelial sodium channel (DEG/ENaC) ppk29 (Liu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Zelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing sei.

claim: sei is located downstream of ppk29
source: Using this approach, we found that the gene seizure (sei), which encodes the sole fly homolog of the human Ether-à-go-go Related Gene (hERG) inward rectifying K+ channel (Titus et al., 1997; Wang et al., 1997), is located downstream of the degenerin/epithelial sodium channel (DEG/ENaC) ppk29 (Liu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Zelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior work.

claim: sei and ppk29 are convergently transcribed on opposite DNA strands
source: The two genes are convergently transcribed on opposite DNA strands, and have complementary 3′UTRs that overlap by 88 nucleotides, which we confirmed by fully sequenced cDNAs deposited in NCBI and 3'RACE analysis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is confirmed by analysis of cDNA sequences and 3'RACE experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: sei and ppk29 have complementary 3′UTRs that overlap by 88 nucleotides
source: The two genes are convergently transcribed on opposite DNA strands, and have complementary 3′UTRs that overlap by 88 nucleotides, which we confirmed by fully sequenced cDNAs deposited in NCBI and 3'RACE analysis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is confirmed by analysis of cDNA sequences and 3'RACE experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: sei and ppk29 are co-expressed in neuronal cell lines
source: Although previous studies suggested that ppk29 function might be a sensory-specific (Liu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012), our analysis revealed that sei and ppk29 are co-expressed in neuronal cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and are both enriched in the fly central nervous system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by expression data from modENcode shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: sei and ppk29 are both enriched in the fly central nervous system
source: Although previous studies suggested that ppk29 function might be a sensory-specific (Liu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012), our analysis revealed that sei and ppk29 are co-expressed in neuronal cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and are both enriched in the fly central nervous system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by expression data from FlyExpress shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In situ hybridization in the fly brain demonstrated neuronal co-expression of sei and ppk29
source: In situ hybridization in the fly brain also demonstrated neuronal co-expression (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization images shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Both sei and ppk29 are co-expressed in motor neurons in vivo
source: Furthermore, we used cell-specific mRNA enrichment (Thomas et al., 2012) to demonstrate that both genes are co-expressed in motor neurons in vivo (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TRAP experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: When animals adapted to high temperature (37°C), the transcript levels of sei went up and ppk29 went down relative to their levels at 25°C
source: In agreement with our hypothesis, we found that when animals adapted to high temperature (37°C) the transcripts levels of sei went up and ppk29 went down relative to their levels at 25°C.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Adaptation to colder temperature (13°C) led to an opposite effect on the expression of sei and ppk29 compared to high temperature adaptation
source: In contrast, adaptation to colder temperature (13°C) led to an opposite effect on the expression of both genes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both sei and ppk29 are likely to play opposite roles in the regulation of neuronal activity in response to changes in ambient temperature
source: We conclude that both sei and ppk29 are likely to play opposite roles in the regulation of neuronal activity in response to changes in ambient temperature, and that the possible interaction between these two genes is physiologically relevant.
evidence: This is inferred from the opposite changes in expression levels at different temperatures (Figure 2) and the opposite behavioral phenotypes (Figure 3A).

claim: Mutations in sei are highly sensitive to heat stress
source: The data presented in Figure 2, and previous reports that indicated that mutations in sei are highly sensitive to heat stress (Titus et al., 1997; Wang et al., 1997), led us to hypothesize that mutations in ppk29 might lead to a protection from heat stress.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Multiple independent mutations in sei lead to rapid seizures and paralysis in response to acute heat stress
source: As was previously reported, we found that multiple independent mutations in sei lead to rapid seizures and paralysis in response to acute heat stress (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 3A.

claim: Flies carrying independent insertional alleles of ppk29 demonstrated protection from the effects of heat stress relative to wild type and sei mutant animals
source: In contrast, flies carrying independent insertional alleles of ppk29 demonstrated protection from the effects of heat stress relative to wild type and sei mutant animals (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B; ppk29P1 and ppk29P2 are described in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: sei and ppk29 play opposing roles in the neuronal response to heat stress
source: These data confirmed our hypothesis that sei and ppk29 play opposing roles in the neuronal response to heat stress, and are likely playing an important adaptive role in environmentally induced neuronal plasticity.
evidence: This is inferred from the opposite behavioral phenotypes of sei and ppk29 mutants shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The temperature-sensitive phenotype of sei mutants is associated with heat-induced neuronal hyperexcitability
source: Previous studies indicated that the temperature-sensitive phenotype of sei mutants is associated with heat-induced neuronal hyperexcitability (Kasbekar et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and confirmed by neurophysiological data in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The spontaneous neuronal activity of larval motor neurons is not different between ppk29, sei and wild type animals at 25°C
source: We found that the spontaneous neuronal activity of larval motor neurons is not different between ppk29, sei and wild type animals at 25°C.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neurophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: At 38°C wild type neurons show a small but significant increase in neuronal activity
source: In contrast, at 38°C wild type neurons show a small but significant increase in neuronal activity, while sei mutant neurons become hyperexcitable.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neurophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: sei mutant neurons become hyperexcitable at 38°C
source: In contrast, at 38°C wild type neurons show a small but significant increase in neuronal activity, while sei mutant neurons become hyperexcitable.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neurophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: ppk29 mutants are unable to increase neuronal firing rates in response to heat stress
source: In contrast to sei null and wild type animals, ppk29 mutants are unable to increase neuronal firing rates in response to heat stress, which is consistent with a hypoexcitability phenotype (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neurophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: At 25°C all genotypes show normal larval locomotion
source: As in our neurophysiological studies, we found that at 25°C all genotypes show normal larval locomotion (Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by videos and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Exposure to 38°C leads to an abnormal seizure-like locomotion in wild type larvae
source: However, exposure to 38°C lead to an abnormal seizure-like locomotion in wild type animals (twitching and rolling).
evidence: This is demonstrated by videos and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The seizure-like locomotion phenotype at 38°C is significantly higher in sei mutant and RNAi knockdown larvae
source: This phenotype is significantly higher in sei mutant and RNAi knockdown larvae but completely absent in ppk29 mutant larvae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F; Videos 4–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by videos and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The seizure-like locomotion phenotype at 38°C is completely absent in ppk29 mutant larvae
source: This phenotype is significantly higher in sei mutant and RNAi knockdown larvae but completely absent in ppk29 mutant larvae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F; Videos 4–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by videos and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: sei and ppk29 affect the behavioral sensitivity to heat stress via the contrasting regulation of neuronal excitability in both larval and adult stages
source: We conclude that sei and ppk29 affect the behavioral sensitivity to heat stress via the contrasting regulation of neuronal excitability in both larval and adult stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral and neurophysiological data in both larvae and adults shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neuronal RNAi-dependent knockdown of sei and ppk29 mRNAs leads to contrasting phenotypes that are identical to the phenotypes observed in mutants
source: Similarly to the mutant adult phenotypes, neuronal RNAi-dependent knockdown of sei and ppk29 mRNAs with the neuronal elav-GAL4 driver lead to contrasting phenotypes that are identical to the phenotypes observed in mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 3D.

claim: The observed phenotypes are neuronal-specific
source: These data demonstrate that the observed phenotypes are neuronal-specific and suggest that quantitative changes in neuronal mRNA levels of either sei or ppk29 are sufficient to induce high-sensitivity or protective phenotypes respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the use of the neuronal-specific elav-GAL4 driver in RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Quantitative changes in neuronal mRNA levels of either sei or ppk29 are sufficient to induce high-sensitivity or protective phenotypes respectively
source: These data demonstrate that the observed phenotypes are neuronal-specific and suggest that quantitative changes in neuronal mRNA levels of either sei or ppk29 are sufficient to induce high-sensitivity or protective phenotypes respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3D and mRNA level measurements in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Downregulation of ppk29 mRNA is associated with increased sei mRNA levels
source: Analyses of mRNA levels in mutants and RNAi-expressing animals support the hypothesis that downregulation of ppk29 mRNA is associated with increased sei mRNA levels, but the converse effect is not evident (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Changes in sei mRNA levels do not affect ppk29 mRNA levels
source: Analyses of mRNA levels in mutants and RNAi-expressing animals support the hypothesis that downregulation of ppk29 mRNA is associated with increased sei mRNA levels, but the converse effect is not evident (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The regulatory interaction between the mRNAs of sei and ppk29 is not symmetric
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the regulatory interaction between the mRNAs of sei and ppk29 is not symmetric; changes in ppk29 mRNA level downregulate sei mRNA, but not the other way around.
evidence: This is inferred from the qRT-PCR data in Figure 3E,F showing asymmetric effects.

claim: The contrasting effects of sei and ppk29 mRNA downregulation on the neuronal response to heat stress are physiological rather than developmental
source: We also observed contrasting phenotypes when we expressed the same gene-specific RNAi constructs in adult neurons only by using the hormonally-induced GeneSwitch version of the elav-GAL4 (Osterwalder et al., 2001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G). These data show that the contrasting effects of sei and ppk29 mRNA dowregulation on the neuronal response to heat stress are physiological rather than developmental.
evidence: This is demonstrated by adult-specific RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: sei or ppk29 mutants do not show general locomotion defects at 25°C
source: We did not observe any general locomotion defects in sei or ppk29 mutants at 25°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by negative geotaxis assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The protective effect of mutations in ppk29 leads to a pre-stress increase in sei transcript levels
source: Together, data presented in Figures 2 and 3 suggest that the protective effect of mutations in ppk29 are symptomatic in the sense that they lead to a pre-stress increase in sei transcript levels, which leads to a higher ability of the nervous system to deal with the acute heat stress even without prior adaptation to slow temperature increase.
evidence: This is inferred from the qRT-PCR data in Figure 3E,F showing increased sei mRNA in ppk29 mutants.

claim: Blocking SEI channel activity in wild type animals phenocopies the heat sensitivity phenotype of the sei mutation
source: These studies reveal that blocking SEI activity in wild type animals phenocopies the heat sensitivity phenotype of the sei mutation, which indicate that the drugs are successfully blocking SEI channels in the fly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking SEI activity in ppk29 mutants reduces their resistance to heat stress to a level comparable to wild type animals in a dose-dependent manner
source: Similar to wild type animals, blocking SEI activity in ppk29 mutants reduce their resistance to heat stress to a level comparable to wild type animals in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ppk29-mediated protection from heat stress is due, at least in part, to increased SEI K+ channel activity rather than the loss of ppk29-dependent Na+ currents
source: These data are in agreement with the expression data (Figure 3E,F), and strongly indicate that the ppk29-mediated protection from heat stress is due, at least in part, to increased SEI K+ channel activity rather then the loss of ppk29-dependent Na+ currents.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological blocking experiments in Figure 4A and the expression data in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Neuronal expression of ppk29-3′UTR is sufficient to rescue the majority of the protective effect of the ppk29 mutation
source: Remarkably, we found that the expression of the ppk29 endogenous 3′UTR alone or the cDNA with the 3′UTR is sufficient to rescue the ppk29 mutation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by transgenic rescue experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of ppk29 cDNA alone is not sufficient to completely rescue the phenotype of the ppk29 mutation
source: In contrast, expression of ppk29 cDNA alone is not sufficient to completely rescue the phenotype of the ppk29 mutation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transgenic rescue experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The main protective effect of ppk29 mutations is mediated via 3′UTR-dependent regulation of SEI, independent of PPK29 channel functions
source: In agreement with the pharmacological studies, these data demonstrate that the main protective effect of ppk29 mutations is mediated via 3′UTR-dependent regulation of SEI, independent of PPK29 channel functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the transgenic rescue experiments in Figure 4C showing that the 3'UTR alone can rescue the phenotype.

claim: PPK29 channel activity may also contribute to neuronal excitability independent of sei regulation
source: Nevertheless, we also found that a complete rescue of the ppk29 mutation phenotype require the expression of the ppk29 cDNA with its endogenous 3′UTR. Therefore, PPK29 channel activity may also contribute neuronal excitability independent of sei regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue by the 3'UTR alone shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The observed effects of ppk29 transgenes on sei function are in trans
source: In addition, since the observed effects of ppk29 transgenes on sei function are in trans, these data show that the two genes can interact at the transcript level independent of their chromosomal proximity.
evidence: This is inferred from the use of transgenes inserted at different chromosomal locations.

claim: The two genes can interact at the transcript level independent of their chromosomal proximity
source: In addition, since the observed effects of ppk29 transgenes on sei function are in trans, these data show that the two genes can interact at the transcript level independent of their chromosomal proximity.
evidence: This is inferred from the transgenic experiments showing trans effects.

claim: Neuronal expression of sei cDNA with or without its endogenous 3′UTR, but not the 3′UTR alone, is sufficient to rescue the sei mutation
source: Unlike for ppk29, the neuronal expression of sei cDNA with or without its endogenous 3′UTR, but not the 3′UTR alone, is sufficient to rescue the sei mutation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transgenic rescue experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: sei is the focal physiological element in the neuronal response to heat stress
source: These data further show that sei is the focal physiological element in the neuronal response to heat stress, and that the mRNA 3′UTR-dependent interaction between sei and ppk29 is not symmetric.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that sei protein is required for function (Figure 4D) and the asymmetric regulatory relationship.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of sei cDNA is sufficient to protect animals from heat stress as in ppk29 mutants
source: Consistent with our model, neuronal overexpression of sei cDNA (with or without its endogenous 3′UTR but not the 3′UTR alone) is sufficient to protect animals from heat stress as in ppk29 mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of a ppk29 cDNA with its endogenous 3′UTR or ppk29 3′UTR alone, but not the cDNA alone, is sufficient to induce heat sensitivity as in sei mutants
source: We also found that neuronal overexpression of a ppk29 cDNA with its endogenous 3′UTR or ppk29 3′UTR alone, but not the cDNA alone, is sufficient to induce heat sensitivity as in sei mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Overexpression of the ppk29-3′UTR is sufficient to reduce endogenous sei mRNA levels
source: In agreement with the behavioral data, overexpression of the ppk29-3′UTR is sufficient to reduce endogenous sei mRNA levels but overexpression of sei-3′UTR alone does not have a similar effect on ppk29 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Overexpression of sei-3′UTR alone does not reduce ppk29 mRNA levels
source: In agreement with the behavioral data, overexpression of the ppk29-3′UTR is sufficient to reduce endogenous sei mRNA levels but overexpression of sei-3′UTR alone does not have a similar effect on ppk29 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Elevated levels of ppk29-3′UTR alone in trans are sufficient to affect neuronal physiology by downregulating sei mRNA levels
source: These data demonstrate that elevated levels of ppk29-3′UTR alone in trans are sufficient to affect neuronal physiology by downregulating sei mRNA levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The observed effects of ppk29-3′UTR overexpression on sei function and behavior are physiological and not developmental
source: Expression of the ppk29 related constructs specifically in the adult nervous system by using the GeneSwitch elav-GAL4 driver demonstrate that the observed effects of ppk29-3′UTR overexpression on sei function and behavior are physiological and not developmental (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by adult-specific inducible expression experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Downregulation of sei expression leads to neuronal heat sensitivity
source: Thus, our data prove that downregulation of sei expression leads to neuronal heat sensitivity while increased sei expression leads to a protection, and that the relative abundance of sei transcripts in neurons is affected by the expression levels of ppk29.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi and overexpression experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Increased sei expression leads to protection from heat stress
source: Thus, our data prove that downregulation of sei expression leads to neuronal heat sensitivity while increased sei expression leads to a protection, and that the relative abundance of sei transcripts in neurons is affected by the expression levels of ppk29.
evidence: This is demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The relative abundance of sei transcripts in neurons is affected by the expression levels of ppk29
source: Thus, our data prove that downregulation of sei expression leads to neuronal heat sensitivity while increased sei expression leads to a protection, and that the relative abundance of sei transcripts in neurons is affected by the expression levels of ppk29.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figures 3E,F and 5C.

claim: The processing of endo-siRNAs depends on Dicer2 (Dcr-2) in flies
source: The processing of endo-siRNAs depends on Dicer2 (Dcr-2) in flies (Czech et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: In the background of the Dcr-2 mutation, neuronal overexpression of the ppk29-3′UTR has no effect on the behavioral response to heat stress
source: We find that in the background of the Dcr-2 mutation neuronal overexpression of the ppk29-3′UTR has no effect on the behavioral response to heat stress (Figure 5E) or on the expression levels of sei (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Dcr-2 mutant background shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the background of the Dcr-2 mutation, neuronal overexpression of the ppk29-3′UTR has no effect on the expression levels of sei
source: We find that in the background of the Dcr-2 mutation neuronal overexpression of the ppk29-3′UTR has no effect on the behavioral response to heat stress (Figure 5E) or on the expression levels of sei (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Dcr-2 mutant background shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The regulatory function of ppk29-3′UTR depends on the endogenous siRNA pathway
source: These data demonstrate that the regulatory function of ppk29-3′UTR depends on the endogenous siRNA pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of function in Dcr-2 mutants shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: RISC treats only one of the strands of dsRNA as a guide
source: Recent studies of the molecular mechanism that underly the specificity of the RNAi machinery indicate that the protein complex that mediate the recognition of the target RNA by the short dsRNA are not symmetrical. Thus, via mechanisms that are not fully understood, RISC treats only one of the strands as a guide (Tomari et al., 2004; Rand et al., 2005; Betancur and Tomari, 2012; Noland and Doudna, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work on RNAi mechanisms.

claim: When forming siRNA duplexes, ppk29 3′UTR is the preferred guide strand during RISC loading and the subsequent mRNA target identification
source: Our data indicate that when forming siRNA duplexes, ppk29 3′UTR is the preferred guide strand during RISC loading and the subsequent mRNA target identification.
evidence: This is inferred from the asymmetric regulatory relationship and the requirement for Dcr-2.

claim: The double-stranded RNA helicase maleless (mle) regulates the Drosophila voltage-gated sodium channel paralytic (para) via A-to-I RNA editing
source: For example, the double-stranded RNA helicase maleless (mle) regulates the Drosophila voltage-gated sodium channel paralytic (para) via A-to-I RNA editing. Mutations in mle lead to aberrant editing of para, splicing errors, and subsequent low channel activity (Reenan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from prior work as an example of RNA-dependent regulation of ion channels.

claim: Mutations in mle lead to aberrant editing of para, splicing errors, and subsequent low channel activity
source: For example, the double-stranded RNA helicase maleless (mle) regulates the Drosophila voltage-gated sodium channel paralytic (para) via A-to-I RNA editing. Mutations in mle lead to aberrant editing of para, splicing errors, and subsequent low channel activity (Reenan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: The putative transcription factor down and out (dao) affects sei transcription levels
source: Other examples include the putative transcription factor down and out (dao), which seem to affect sei transcription levels (Fergestad et al., 2010), the potassium-independent effects of the sei-related mammalian EAG potassium channel on cellular signaling (Hegle et al., 2006), and other diverse mechanisms for the co-regulation of various ion channels (MacLean et al., 2005; Ransdell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior work as another example of ion channel regulation.

claim: The sei-related mammalian EAG potassium channel has potassium-independent effects on cellular signaling
source: Other examples include the putative transcription factor down and out (dao), which seem to affect sei transcription levels (Fergestad et al., 2010), the potassium-independent effects of the sei-related mammalian EAG potassium channel on cellular signaling (Hegle et al., 2006), and other diverse mechanisms for the co-regulation of various ion channels (MacLean et al., 2005; Ransdell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: At least two of the three fly eag-like (KCNH-type) channels are organized in a chromosomal architecture that is similar to that of sei and ppk29
source: Bioinformatic analyses of genome sequences show that at least two of the three fly and three out of the eight human eag-like (KCNH-type) channels are organized in a chromosomal architecture that is similar to that of sei and ppk29 (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: Three out of the eight human eag-like (KCNH-type) channels are organized in a chromosomal architecture that is similar to that of sei and ppk29
source: Bioinformatic analyses of genome sequences show that at least two of the three fly and three out of the eight human eag-like (KCNH-type) channels are organized in a chromosomal architecture that is similar to that of sei and ppk29 (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: The regulatory interaction between sei and ppk29 may play a role in the homeostatic response to slow changes in environmental temperature
source: Our findings also indicate that the regulatory interaction between sei and ppk29 may play a role in the homeostatic response to slow changes in environmental temperature (Figure 2).
evidence: This is speculated based on the temperature adaptation data in Figure 2.

claim: mRNAs can serve as regulatory RNAs, independent of their protein-coding capacity
source: In this regard, our studies provide an additional layer of regulatory complexity, and support the idea that mRNAs, which are typically thought to solely act as the template for protein translation, can also serve as regulatory RNAs, independent of their protein-coding capacity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data showing 3'UTR-dependent regulation.

claim: The abundance of convergent transcription of protein-coding genes in eukaryotic genomes suggests that many other mRNAs might serve dual functions
source: Thus, the abundance of convergent transcription of protein-coding genes in eukaryotic genomes suggests that many other mRNAs might serve dual functions that are not necessary associated with the same cellular or physiological processes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of this study and the prevalence of convergent transcription.

claim: The mRNA-dependent interaction between sei and ppk29 occurs in cis
source: Furthermore, although the phenomenon of mRNA-dependent interaction between the two genes we describe here occurs in cis (Figure 6), we currently have no reason to assume that similar interactions between RNAs cannot occur in trans as well.
evidence: This is based on the chromosomal organization shown in Figure 6, though trans effects are also demonstrated.

claim: Similar RNA-RNA interactions can occur in trans
source: Furthermore, although the phenomenon of mRNA-dependent interaction between the two genes we describe here occurs in cis (Figure 6), we currently have no reason to assume that similar interactions between RNAs cannot occur in trans as well.
evidence: This is speculated based on the trans effects observed with transgenes.

claim: Some evolutionary changes observed in mRNAs that are considered 'neutral' should be re-evaluated in light of the possible regulatory function that some mRNAs might exert independently of the proteins they encode
source: Consequently, it is likely that some of the evolutionary changes observed in mRNAs, including those that are considered 'neutral', should be re-evaluated in light of the possible regulatory function that some mRNAs might exert independently of the proteins they encode.
evidence: This is speculated based on the implications of the findings.

claim: The 3'UTRs of sei and ppk29 overlap by 88 nucleotides as confirmed by fully sequenced cDNAs deposited in NCBI
source: The two genes are convergently transcribed on opposite DNA strands, and have complementary 3′UTRs that overlap by 88 nucleotides, which we confirmed by fully sequenced cDNAs deposited in NCBI and 3'RACE analysis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is confirmed by analysis of deposited cDNA sequences (AY058350 for sei and BT029266 for ppk29) shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The 3'UTRs of sei and ppk29 overlap by 88 nucleotides as confirmed by 3'RACE analysis
source: The two genes are convergently transcribed on opposite DNA strands, and have complementary 3′UTRs that overlap by 88 nucleotides, which we confirmed by fully sequenced cDNAs deposited in NCBI and 3'RACE analysis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is confirmed by 3'RACE experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ppk29 function might be sensory-specific according to previous studies
source: Although previous studies suggested that ppk29 function might be a sensory-specific (Liu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012), our analysis revealed that sei and ppk29 are co-expressed in neuronal cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and are both enriched in the fly central nervous system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is cited from prior work but contradicted by the current study's findings.

claim: Blocking SEI channel activity in wild type animals with hERG channel blockers reduces time to heat-induced paralysis
source: These studies reveal that blocking SEI activity in wild type animals phenocopies the heat sensitivity phenotype of the sei mutation, which indicate that the drugs are successfully blocking SEI channels in the fly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the pharmacological experiments in Figure 4A showing reduced time to paralysis with drug treatment.

claim: The complementary 3'UTRs of sei and ppk29 mRNAs can form a dsRNA
source: The chromosomal organization of these two genes suggest they could generate endogenous siRNA by convergent transcription. (I) The complementary 3′UTRs of sei and ppk29 mRNAs form a dsRNA.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 6 and supported by the overlap data.

claim: Dicer-2 cleaves dsRNAs formed by sei and ppk29 3'UTRs into siRNAs
source: (II) Dicer-2 cleaves dsRNAs into siRNAs.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 6 and supported by the Dcr-2 requirement shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The loaded RISC complex targets sei transcripts for degradation via the canonical siRNA pathway
source: (III) The loaded RISC complex targets sei transcripts for degradation via the canonical siRNA pathway.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 6 and supported by the Dcr-2 requirement and the reduction in sei mRNA levels.
